clinicalPearls: A systemic vasculitis presenting with various combinations of oral and genital ulcers, skin lesions, uveitis, arthritis, large vessel (arterial and venous) disease, and gastrointestinal and neurologic involvement, with manifestations appearing in differing sequences over time.

Oral ulcers occur in essentially all patients (~98%) and are usually the first manifestation; they are typically multiple, resemble ordinary canker sores, last about 10 days, and recur unless treated, with only the uncommon major ulcers tending to scar.
Genital ulcers are the most specific lesion, most often on the scrotum or labia; they are larger, deeper, slower to heal than oral ulcers, and tend to scar.
The pathergy reaction (a papule or pustule forming 24-48 h after a needle prick) is a fairly unique nonspecific skin hyperreactivity and is part of the diagnostic criteria.
Hypopyon (intense anterior chamber inflammation), seen in about 10% of patients with eye disease, is quite specific for Behçet syndrome.
Superficial thrombophlebitis often occurs in men and is associated with deep-vein thrombosis; its presence should prompt a workup for other vascular involvement including pulmonary artery aneurysm.
HLA-B*51 is positive in up to 50-60% of patients depending on geographic origin, but it is not diagnostic because roughly 20% of the normal population also carries it.
Most prevalent in Turkey (about 1 in 250 adults); patients are most commonly from the Middle East, Mediterranean, and Far East. Onset before the late teens or after age 50 is uncommon.
Sexes are affected roughly equally, but males tend to have more severe disease and worse outcomes; eye involvement may reach ~70% in males.
Ocular disease (most often bilateral panuveitis) usually appears within the first 2 years after diagnostic criteria are met, is most severe early, then tends to abate.
Most new manifestations appear within the first 5 years, and the natural history for most patients is one of diminishing symptoms that may culminate in remission.
reference.pathophysiology: The cause and pathogenesis are unknown. Family studies suggest a possible genetic predisposition, and heightened inflammation with involvement of both innate and adaptive immunity is implicated. Neutrophil hyperreactivity is present, though it is unclear whether this is primary or secondary to cytokine-driven activation. The disorder sits between classic autoimmune and autoinflammatory conditions: unlike typical autoimmune disease it is not generally associated with autoantibodies, Raynaud's phenomenon, Sjögren's syndrome, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, photosensitivity, serosal involvement, or increased risk of other autoimmune diseases; unlike classic autoinflammatory disease it tends to abate over time, lacks the mutations seen in autoinflammatory syndromes, and is more prevalent than disorders such as familial Mediterranean fever. Retrospective cohort data suggest distinct disease clusters (e.g., acne lesions clustering with arthritis and enthesitis) that may have differing pathogeneses.
additionalDifferentials: Crohn's disease (gastrointestinal Behçet can be clinically and endoscopically indistinguishable; distinction often relies on extraintestinal features)
Recurrent aphthous stomatitis / ordinary canker sores
Acne vulgaris (papulopustular lesions are indistinguishable in appearance and pathology)
infectionMimics: Herpetic and other infectious genital/oral ulceration causing recurrent ulcers
additionalInvestigations: Diagnosis is clinical; no specific laboratory, imaging, or histologic test confirms it, so investigations mainly serve to exclude mimics.

International Study Group (ISG) criteria: recurrent oral ulceration (at least 3 times in 12 months) plus two of recurrent genital ulcers, skin lesions, eye lesions, or a positive pathergy test (sensitivity ~95%, specificity ~96%).
Pathergy test: dermal insertion of a 20-gauge (20-21 gauge) needle, read at 24-48 h.
HLA-B*51 testing may support but cannot establish the diagnosis.
Endoscopy for suspected gastrointestinal involvement (ulcers typically single or fewer than five, deep, round, confined to the ileocecal area, prone to perforation).
Vascular and neuroimaging when vascular or CNS involvement is suspected (e.g., pulmonary artery aneurysm, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, parenchymal CNS lesions).
redFlags: Superficial thrombophlebitis in a male should trigger evaluation for deeper vascular involvement including pulmonary artery aneurysm.
Pulmonary artery aneurysms carry a 5-year mortality of about 20-25%.
Subacute severe headache with cranial nerve palsy, dysarthria, ataxia, or hemiparesis suggests parenchymal CNS involvement (telencephalic-diencephalic junction, brainstem, spinal cord).
Deep, round ileocecal ulcers are prone to perforation.
Clustering thrombotic events (deep-vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, IVC syndrome, intracardiac thrombosis, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis).
reference.prognosis: Most patients follow a course of diminishing symptoms over time with potential remission, often eventually requiring no ongoing medication, and most new manifestations emerge within the first 5 years. Young male patients tend to have worse outcomes. Poor ocular prognostic factors include male sex, posterior involvement, frequent attacks (>3 per year), strong vitreous opacity, and macular edema. Pulmonary artery aneurysms are associated with a 5-year mortality of about 20-25%.
pitfalls: Diagnosis may take months to years as the full constellation of features evolves; a tentative diagnosis often precedes a definitive one.
HLA-B*51 is not a diagnostic test because it is common in the general population.
Gastrointestinal Behçet is easily mistaken for Crohn's disease unless extraintestinal manifestations are evident.
Pathergy and eye lesions each occur in only about half of patients, so their absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
Regional variation matters: gastrointestinal involvement is common in Japan and seen in ~30% of US patients but rare in Turkey.
reference.severityClassification: No formal severity grade; management and outlook are stratified by the type and severity of organ involvement (mucocutaneous, ocular, vascular, gastrointestinal, neurologic), with young male sex and posterior/severe eye disease marking higher-risk disease.
management: Treat mucocutaneous disease with topical corticosteroids for oral and genital ulcers and colchicine for mucocutaneous lesions and arthritis, adding apremilast for resistant oral ulceration

Manage sight-threatening uveitis and retinal vasculitis with systemic corticosteroids plus immunosuppression such as azathioprine or ciclosporin, escalating to TNF-alpha inhibitors (infliximab or adalimumab) or interferon-alpha
Use corticosteroids with an immunosuppressant such as azathioprine or cyclophosphamide, or a biologic, for major organ involvement

Treat vascular thrombosis primarily with immunosuppression for the underlying inflammation rather than anticoagulation alone, and manage arterial and pulmonary artery aneurysms with immunosuppression and considered intervention
Manage gastrointestinal disease with corticosteroids, aminosalicylates, azathioprine or anti-TNF therapy, watching for perforation
Treat parenchymal neuro-Behcet with corticosteroids and immunosuppression, avoiding ciclosporin because of neurotoxicity
Coordinate multidisciplinary care with ophthalmology, rheumatology and relevant organ specialists, escalating early in organ-threatening disease
